segments.title: Westerwald tests Norwegian neutrality
segments.summary: A day-by-day naval chronology follows the German supply ship Westerwald through Norwegian waters, where neutrality depended on balancing pressure from both belligerents.
segments.body: The first book is a large chronological reference for the naval war of 1939-45. Its November 1939 example follows the German supply ship Westerwald after it replenished Deutschland in the North Atlantic and Norwegian torpedo boats stopped it on the way home. German diplomatic pressure secured the ship's passage through Norwegian waters, establishing a precedent before the better-known Altmark incident. No Royal Navy ship was present to block the passage, leaving Norway to handle the confrontation while trying to keep both belligerents balanced. The incident shows how limited naval power made neutrality difficult to enforce.

evidence.note: The book's November 1939 entry and the Norwegian neutrality dilemma are discussed.

segments.title: Norway 1940 through a dense naval chronology
segments.summary: The Norwegian campaign entry links Renown, Narvik, coastal batteries, troop landings, and the loss of Blücher into one fast-moving operational picture.
segments.body: The chronology moves from Renown's engagement with Gneisenau and Scharnhorst to the German landing groups and Norway's scattered coastal defences. An aside questions Renown's usual battlecruiser label and suggests that the ship is better understood as a light battleship. Two German 28-centimetre shells that struck Renown failed to explode, while a 15-inch hit damaged Gneisenau's fire-control position. The invasion narrative then shifts among batteries, torpedo boats, submarines, fog, aircraft, and troops landing at several ports. Blücher's destruction in the Drøbak Narrows stands beside smaller actions and captured Norwegian craft. The chronology makes clear how much of the campaign unfolded beyond its best-known incidents.

evidence.note: The chronology's 9 April Norway entries cover Renown, Narvik, landing groups, coastal batteries, and Blücher.

segments.title: An accessible visual overview of war at sea
segments.summary: The second book is recommended as a map- and illustration-rich introduction to naval war from 1914 to 1945.
segments.body: The volume gives a quick overview through maps, pictures, and concise text. It spans both world wars and gives the interwar period a shorter treatment. It is an introductory guide rather than a final authority: readers may disagree with individual interpretations, but it offers a practical sense of what was happening. Its chief value is orientation and visual explanation rather than an account whose every claim must be accepted.

evidence.note: The review describes the book's maps, pictures, introductory value, and 1914–45 scope.

segments.title: Treaty limits turn design into a chain of compromises
segments.summary: Carrier, Town-class, and Crown Colony-class design compromises show the price of displacement limits, while Bismarck and Tirpitz illustrate the advantage claimed for exceeding them.
segments.body: A passage on carrier design argues that better appreciation of the bombing threat led to more horizontal protection. Keeping displacement fixed meant that the added protection reduced aircraft capacity. The review then contrasts expensive 9,400-ton Town-class cruisers with cramped 8,000-ton Crown Colony-class ships that tried to retain similar offensive power. Bismarck and Tirpitz provide the opposite case: the book says they exceeded their official displacement by more than 10,000 tons and argues that the breach paid off in action. These examples connect treaty compliance directly to protection, aircraft capacity, firepower, and living space.

evidence.note: The cited examples connect carrier protection and air-group capacity with cruiser displacement, cramped layouts, and the excess displacement of Bismarck and Tirpitz.

segments.title: Magnetic mines turn coastal channels into wreck fields
segments.summary: An image of wreck-strewn East Coast channels conveys the immediate maritime danger created by the 1940 magnetic-mine campaign.
segments.body: The book's photographs make the mine threat tangible. Shallow British East Coast channels were filled with half-submerged wrecks during the height of the magnetic-mine campaign. The Union-Castle liner Dunbar Castle was an early January 1940 casualty off North Foreland. The example shows how mine warfare could disrupt ordinary coastal movement and turn constrained shipping channels into persistent hazards.

evidence.note: The review describes wrecks in East Coast channels during the magnetic-mine campaign and the Dunbar Castle loss.

segments.title: A global, three-dimensional naval view of the First World War
segments.summary: Norman Friedman's First World War study is introduced as a global naval history where aircraft and submarines reshape strategy, operations, tactics, and technology.
segments.body: The third book shifts attention away from an exclusively Western Front view of the First World War and back to the conflict at sea around the world. Norman Friedman's account connects strategy with technology instead of treating either in isolation. Aircraft and submarines make the maritime battlespace three-dimensional. Their emergence begins a revolution in strategy, operations, tactics, and technology both at sea and from the sea.

evidence.note: The review introduces the book's global scope and its treatment of aircraft, submarines, strategy, and technology.

segments.title: Fleet superiority must allow for ships in refit
segments.summary: A discussion of British naval policy explains why a paper advantage over an enemy fleet must be large enough to absorb refits and unavailable ships.
segments.body: The review traces how the Royal Navy's planning benchmark shifted from the next two powers to Germany as diplomatic alignments changed. The proposed 60 percent margin rests on an availability problem: a fleet cannot assume every hull is ready when an opponent chooses the moment to sail. Ships in refit or too distant to concentrate reduce the usable share of the nominal fleet, while the enemy can time a sortie for high availability. Maintenance and distance reduce what a fleet can actually deploy, so numerical superiority becomes a force-structure problem rather than a simple hull count.

evidence.note: The passage explains the two-power standard, the German comparison, and the availability logic behind a larger British margin.

segments.title: German navy laws and the cost of capital ships
segments.summary: The German Navy Laws locked in battleship numbers, pushing fiscal pressure onto personnel, torpedoes, and the size and cost of individual ships.
segments.body: Tirpitz's naval programme fixed the number of battleships and limited the freedom to trade quantity against the quality or cost of individual ships. As dreadnoughts became more expensive, the resulting fiscal pressure appeared in cuts to personnel and other non-procurement spending. Friedman also points to inadequate torpedoes as one operational consequence. A photograph of Westfalen introduces the Nassau class, whose 11-inch guns held down ship size and cost when contemporary British and other foreign battleships carried 12-inch weapons.

evidence.note: The passage links the Navy Laws, fiscal pressure, torpedoes, the Nassau class, and the cost-saving choice of 11-inch guns.

segments.title: Growing battle ranges favour big-gun armament
segments.summary: Tirpitz rejected more numerous smaller guns because increasing engagement ranges would make them ineffective, challenging a simple story of German preference for lighter weapons.
segments.body: Friedman's account distinguishes the decision to fit 11-inch guns for economy from a broader tactical preference for small-calibre battleship armament. Tirpitz considered using more guns of smaller calibre but rejected the idea. As expected battle ranges increased, those weapons would become ineffective before heavier guns did. That reasoning challenges the claim that German designers simply believed smaller guns were inherently better.

evidence.note: The passage says Tirpitz rejected more numerous smaller guns because increasing gunnery ranges would make them ineffective.

segments.title: A naval atlas for seeing the war in space
segments.summary: Marcus Faulkner's naval atlas is recommended for readers who want a visual, spatial overview of the Second World War at sea.
segments.body: Pictures and maps carry more of the final book's explanation than long passages of prose. They give readers a spatial overview of the 1939-45 naval war and show where events and campaigns unfolded. The review mentions colleagues disputing small details, including plotted positions that may be off by a couple of degrees. Those disagreements do not outweigh the atlas's value as a visual guide.

evidence.note: The review introduces the naval atlas and stresses its visual, spatial presentation of the war.

segments.title: Cape Matapan: aircraft, radar, and a decisive night action
segments.summary: The atlas account of Cape Matapan follows the Italian withdrawal, air attacks on Vittorio Veneto and Pola, radar contact, and British night gunnery.
segments.body: Cape Matapan developed through reconnaissance, speed, air attack, and information before the British battle line opened fire. Vittorio Veneto initially gave the Italians a 28-knot to 21-knot speed advantage, while conflicting reports led Admiral Iachino to underestimate how close the British fleet was. Carrier aircraft and RAF Blenheims damaged the battleship, and an air-dropped torpedo stopped Pola and drew other Italian cruisers back to help. British radar and night training then brought the battleships into point-blank range, where the cruisers were rapidly wrecked. Cunningham turned away to prevent friendly fire among separated British forces, which allowed the remaining Italian ships to escape. The defeat damaged Italian naval morale and helped confine later fleet operations to waters covered by land-based aircraft.

evidence.note: The review recounts the Cape Matapan pursuit, air strikes, radar contact, night gunfire, and the aftermath for the Italian fleet.
